{"notes": "Visit 1 (0:00-1:00). Only 2 dominoes are connected to start, so little built yet. I don't know who placed them, so I'm not crediting anyone.

Priya: Set direction fast (big, simple fish), delegated clearly (bin runs, top line, bottom line, tail, tray for Leo), and sketched the plan (fish facing left). Good leadership and clarity so far. Her instructions were specific and sequenced. Still to see: does she build as well as direct, and does she adapt if things go wrong? Tentative: leadership strong.

Tom: Acknowledged quickly, went for the bin load, and said he'd trace the top line and lay the start domino. Cooperative and responsive. His praise of the sketch was supportive but generic. Watch whether he follows through. The start domino is critical because only what's connected to it falls. Check the start is linked to the fish body.

Maya: Echoed the plan and went to fetch the bin load. Cooperative. Assigned the bottom line. Nothing yet on execution. Watch for follow-through.

Leo: Said nothing while I was there. He was told to grab a tray for himself, but I didn't see him do it or acknowledge. Don't judge yet. He may have been working quietly or may be disengaged or unclear on his role. Priya gave him no build task beyond the tray. Check in on him next visit and ask him privately how he's finding it.

Next visit: check line connectivity to start, who is building, whether Leo is included, and whether the top and bottom lines meet at the tail."}

{"notes": "Visit 2 (2:45). State of table: the dark chain connected to start runs along the bottom line only, to about x=14 of a roughly x=23 fish. The top line is fully laid out to the tail end (x~23.5) but is still pale and unconnected, with a small gap at the nose. Neat spacing and smooth curves overall. I don't know who placed which dominoes, so I'm not crediting placement from the picture.

Priya: Said plainly that the top line wasn't hooked to the start and that she was fixing it at the nose. That's honest status reporting and she took ownership of the critical link. She also handed Tom the upper tail from the far end, a clear and sensible delegation. Leadership still strong. Still unseen: whether she builds as much as she directs. Check the nose join has actually landed next visit.

Maya: Gave a clear status update and committed to calling out when the bottom line reaches the tail. Good communication and reliability. Bottom line is connected to start, but only about halfway, so pace is a watch item with 7 minutes left. She thanked Leo, which is a good collaboration signal.

Tom: Heard nothing from him this visit. He was assigned the upper tail; I don't know if he acknowledged or started. He was also supposed to lay the start domino, and the start is connected to the bottom line, which is a good sign but not proof. Ask what he's working on.

Leo: Maya thanked him, so he contributed something, probably supplies, but I didn't see what. Good sign he's engaged. Still has no real build task. Ask him privately how it's going and whether he wants more to do.

Next visit: Is the top line connected to the start? Is the bottom line keeping pace? Do both lines meet at the tail? Tom's tail progress? Leo's role?"}

{"notes": "Visit 3 (4:00). Table: dark chain from start now runs along the bottom line to the tail (x~23) and also a short stub up toward the nose (x~9, y~9). The top line is fully laid out to the tail but still pale: the nose joint has NOT caught, so the top line isn't connected. Spacing and curves still neat. Two lines don't meet at the tail yet; ~6 min gone, little time left. I still don't know who placed which dominoes, so no placement credit from the picture.

Priya: Said at 3:30 the nose is hooked in and she's checking the whole run. That claim was wrong or premature: the top is still pale. Not dishonest, but she reported success before verifying. Testing the run is a good instinct. Watch whether she fixes the joint now or just re-tests. Leadership still decent, execution on the nose link is a concern.

Tom: Reported upper tail is down, and he noticed the top is still pale so the nose joint isn't catching, and offered to help Priya. Accurate, honest status, follows through on his assigned task, collaborative. Good move. Upgrade view on him.

Maya: Said nothing this visit. Bottom line reached the tail, so she delivered on pace and her earlier promise, though I didn't hear the call-out. Credit tentatively, since I can't confirm who built it.

Leo: Nothing seen or heard again. Still no clear role. Ask him privately what he's done.

Next: Is the nose gap closed and the top line dark? Do both meet at the tail? Did Priya and Tom fix the joint rather than just discuss it?"}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I fetched a full 40-domino load for the shared bin early on, which kept the table supplied while the fish was going up. I laid the upper tail (stroke 3) onto the top line, so the fish has its tail fin on the upper side. In the final minutes I carried the start line on from its live end, curving it up to catch the top line, and that is what got the run catching from the start. Afterward about 88 of the 93 standing dominoes fell from the start, and the fish outline was complete.

Execution: I worked in steady batches of two or three dominoes, checking as I went. When the upper tail showed pale, I inspected the nose joint closely, worked out why it wasn't catching, and bridged it with a gentle curve. I inspected again once the nose was fixed. After that I kept my hands off the nose, as agreed, so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration: I confirmed the plan out loud, worked alongside Priya on the nose, and stayed clear of other people's areas so we didn't bump each other. I kept my updates short and clear, and I backed the hands-off call near the end.

Leadership: I committed to my part early and delivered it, told the table where I was and what I was changing, and helped steer us to a clean, stable finish rather than risky last-minute tinkering. I helped the table reach a good result: a clear fish outline that was almost entirely connected to the start.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I supplied a full 40-domino load to the shared bin in the first minute, so the whole table could start building right away. I then laid the bottom line of the fish, the long lower outline that gives the body its shape. It was finished and connected to the start well before the 5-minute call. Before the push, about 88 of the 93 standing dominoes were connected to the start, and the bottom line was part of that.

Execution: I took the bottom line and traced it steadily from the pad sketch, laying a few dominoes at a time from the start line near the nose. I ran close inspections at 4:15, 4:30 and 5:00 and a final whole-run check. These confirmed that both lines and both tails were dark, and that the only unconnected dominoes were a few strays in the nose that don't touch the outline. After that I kept my hands off, so I didn't risk bumping the finished work.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed throughout, saying when I was on the bottom line, when it was done, and what my checks showed. I stayed clear of the nose once it was agreed to be hands-off, which avoided crowding. I also helped the team agree to stop adjusting and let the fish ride.

Leadership: I took ownership of the bottom line without being chased and reported its status. I also ran the final verification and called the hands-off decision, so the team went into the push with a clear, shared picture of the run's state. I also kept the mood light and positive as the clock ran down.

Overall, I believe I carried a substantial share of the result through the bin supply, the bottom line and the verification checks.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I set the direction at the start of the activity. I chose a fish because its outline is simple and recognizable, and I sketched it on the pad: nose on the left, a smooth top and bottom line, and two tails. The sketch was a single run that splits at the nose, so one push could carry the whole thing. Before the push, our final checks showed nearly the whole run connected to the start. That makes me confident the fish read clearly.

Execution
I laid the start domino and traced the top line, the stroke that leaves the start and anchors the rest of the picture. I inspected the nose and the whole run several times to see what the push would actually knock over. I used those checks to tell the table where the pale leftovers were and that they didn't touch the outline. Once the run was connected, I called for hands off so nothing got bumped before the push.

Collaboration
I split the work early and by name. Tom took the upper tail, Maya the bottom line, and Leo the lower tail, with the bin stocked by several people. That let four people build in parallel without crowding each other. I kept the table updated on the state of the run and asked everyone to stay clear of the nose once it was catching, which kept the work in that area from colliding.

Leadership
I made the key decisions quickly: the animal, the design, and who built what. I kept the table calm and focused through the middle stretch. When the run was connected, I helped bring everyone to a clear hands-off decision. We finished with a complete fish standing and ready for the push.", "my_share_percent": 35}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I kept the table supplied so the builders never had to stop. I made two full 40-domino runs to the boxes, 80 dominoes into the shared bin. Big batches cost about 60 seconds per trip, which is much cheaper per domino than small ones. I also built the lower tail of the fish (stroke 4), 14 dominoes traced from the bottom line out to its tip. That finished the tail, which is one of the features that makes the outline read as a fish. Before the push, the run was tracing as roughly 88 of 93 standing dominoes connected to the start.

Execution
I took the lower tail when Priya asked and kept to it, laying it in short steady bursts. I reported progress honestly (ten of fourteen, then done) so the others could plan around it. The tail reached its end and looked dark, meaning connected, all the way from the bump. After that I kept spare dominoes ready in case a patch was needed.

Collaboration
I answered every request directly, confirmed my assignment and kept the others updated on my progress. I stayed out of the nose area once it was marked hands-off. Two people working close together risk bumping each other's lines, so keeping clear protected the work already standing. I did not add anything that could disturb the connected run in the final minutes.

Leadership
My leadership was mostly in supporting the plan. I committed to the lower tail, finished it ahead of the 5-minute mark, and kept the supply from becoming a bottleneck. I stayed disciplined once the picture was complete: hands off, no unnecessary changes. I believe the fish was built efficiently as a team, with my part being the supply and the lower tail.", "my_share_percent": 25}
